articleTitle: Accelerating Post-Tornado Disaster Assessment Using Advanced Deep Learning Models
abstract: Post-disaster assessments of buildings and infrastructure are crucial for both immediate recovery efforts and long-term resilience planning. This research introduces an innovative approach to automating post-disaster assessments through advanced deep learning models. Our proposed system employs state-of-the-art computer vision techniques— YOLOv11 and ResNet50—to rapidly analyze images and videos from disaster sites, extracting critical information about building characteristics, including damage level of structural components and the extent of damage. Our experimental results show promising performance, with ResNet50 achieving 90.28% accuracy and an inference time of 1529ms per image on multiclass damage classification. This study contributes to the field of disaster management by offering a scalable, efficient, and objective tool for post-disaster analysis, potentially capable of transforming how communities and authorities respond to and learn from catastrophic events.

articleTitle: Automated Cycling System for Characterizing Ink-Jet Printed Flexible Films for Sensors
abstract: Reliability testing of electronic devices is vital; anything from temperature and humidity resistance to mechanical fatigue of materials needs to be tested to ensure devices can hold up to their needed life expectancy— particularly in the field of biosensors and flexible conductors. Unfortunately, the research for specific techniques can be scarce, and often devices need to be tested in their own unique way. In this work, we have developed an automated system for reliability testing of strain-dependent sensors through the cyclic bending of a polyimide substrate with a conductive graphene film. A device was created using a 180-degree servo motor in combination with an Arduino microcontroller. The servo motor was then paired with a rack and pinion gear set to function as a linear actuator and bound to an independently built sliding mechanism that serves as the control and measurement of repeated bending operations. The substrate with the graphene film was then attached to a source meter to measure the current flow in situ over time. Subsequently, this device was able to repeat multiple bend cycles identically, eliminating the need to do it by hand and creating uniformity toward data gathering for comparative experimental studies. As such, the automated cycling system fulfilled its purpose towards a reliability test for which the graphene film showed the ability to withstand fatigue through repeated loading.

articleTitle: Integration of Graphene Oxide with Resonant RF Structures for Wireless Humidity Sensing
abstract: The exponential progression of the fourth industrial revolution has transformed the way in which individuals live and work on the Internet of Things (IoT) era. At the heart of IoT is the concept of wireless sensing, a key facilitator for data-driven decisions in autonomous systems and the digitization revolution. Many traditional sensors rely on resistive and capacitive changes to sense environmental makers for which DC conductivity is often measured and the data are then transmitted through additional external communication circuitry. This research employs Radio Frequency (RF) technology, which epitomizes a contemporary advancement in sensor design and allows wireless sensing without external circuitry. Here, we employ a two-dimensional (2D) derivative to graphene which is functionalized with oxygen to yield graphene oxide (GO) membranes, as a sensing material to measure environmental changes in ambient humidity. An RF copper antenna was fabricated on oxidized Silicon substrates which serves as a wireless transmitter, while hydrophilic GO atop the copper antenna serves as a dielectric medium. Due to its hydrophilic nature, GO changes its dielectric permittivity as the ambient humidity changes in the environment, which in turn alters the overall dielectric property of the device and shifts the resonance frequency of the antenna-GO ensemble. We show that the return loss of the antenna-GO ensemble serves as a means to measure environmental humidity and quantify its sensing behavior.

articleTitle: Enhanced Smart Crop Health Monitoring Using Visual Sensors and Image Processing
abstract: The main goal of this research is to explore and apply newer solutions for modernizing the agricultural industry which would effectively contribute to the sustainability and well-being of the society. Our objective is to investigate and implement smart-connected and cost-effective technologies that can aid with efficient crop management. Such solutions can further enable smart decision-making and aid in the automation of certain operations in the agricultural process. In this work, we developed a monitoring system using wireless sensor networks and RGB cameras, with an emphasis on implementing the suitable image processing techniques for monitoring certain features of the crop. We present our preliminary results showing the success of our solution at estimating leaf density and tip burns. This information, and in conjunction with other measurements, can enable smart decision-making and aid in the automation of certain operations in the agricultural process.

articleTitle: Scalable, Low-cost Fabrication of CVD-grown WSe2 for Optoelectronic Devices
abstract: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), including WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> often show unique and exciting optical and electrical features. WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> is well-suited for high-performance optoelectronic devices, such as photodetectors due to its intense photoluminescence properties. This study investigates the production of monolayer WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> using vapor growth approaches and subsequently the fabrication of optoelectronic devices manufactured using low-cost optical lithography. The monolayer membranes were synthesized using low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), which is a method for growing high-quality crystals on dielectric substrates. The use of halide salts allowed tungsten trioxide precursor reduction at lower temperatures, which improved the crystal formation process. Raman and photoluminescence spectroscopy revealed the monolayer nature of the synthesized WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>. Raman peaks were prominent and intense photoluminescence occurred at 1.60 eV. The electrical properties of the manufactured WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> photodetector devices with Ti contacts were evaluated under various situations. Optical lithography was used to create scalable optoelectronic devices from WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> monolayer material through high-throughput approaches such as optical lithography.

articleTitle: Manufacturing WSe2 optoelectronic membrane-based devices using low-cost optical lithography
abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) such as tungsten diselenide (WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) exhibit exceptional optoelectronic properties that can be explored for sensing applications using simplified device architectures. In this study, we report a WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-based photodetector using minimally complex fabrication processes, including mechanical exfoliation of WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and manual mask alignment for photolithography. The device was characterized through electrical transport measurements under ambient and cryogenic conditions. Illumination-dependent analysis revealed a photocurrent enhancement factor of approximately 10 times when measured in vacuum compared to ambient conditions while at room temperature and equivalent photoexcitation conditions. Our findings through this study, validate the feasibility of fabricating WSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-based devices, including photodetectors, using simplified fabrication methodologies, in contrast to complicated processes such as e-beam lithography. This approach offers potential for the development of cost-effective manufacturing approaches for optoelectronic devices based on two-dimensional materials.

articleTitle: Optimizing Data Efficiency and Visual Quality with Intelligent Thresholding in Color Encoding
abstract: Effectively balancing visual representation with data reduction is a central challenge in color reduction encoding. While recent advancements have improved visual quality, the key question is how much information can be safely removed without degrading the image. The proposed smart thresholding method addresses this challenge by using an L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-informationbased approach of optimal data retention. By setting a noise limit threshold, essential image details are preserved while eliminating redundant data. Through the application of L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-norm PCA, the algorithm identifies the point where further color reduction significantly impacts quality, offering an optimal balance between computational efficiency and performance. This approach is crucial for achieving target quantization levels without sacrificing vital image features.

articleTitle: Enhancing Haptic Fingertip Feedback via Pneumatic Actuators
abstract: In this work, we present the design and proof-of-concept for a soft pneumatic actuator that employs a pneumatic transmission to provide haptic feedback to four areas of the fingerpad. With this feedback, users can sense where force is applied on a remote palpation tool. The pneumatic actuator’s performance was evaluated through two preliminary experiments: one measuring force versus pressure and a second assessing participants’ ability to discriminate cues felt on different areas of their fingerpad through the device. Three participants were all able to identify which chamber was being activated with 100% accuracy at a pressure selected for easy identification; even at a second lower pressure, participants averaged 99.2% of chambers correctly identified, with a mean information transfer of 1.95 bits, indicating that it was very easy for participants to distinguish which part of their fingertip was being cued. This passive pneumatic feedback method has potential for applications in soft robotics, haptics, and medical robotics as its ability to provide force feedback could be leveraged in various fields requiring control.

articleTitle: A Smart Insole for Remote Gait Monitoring of Paralyzed Patients
abstract: Paralysis occurs when the nervous system is disrupted, preventing patients from making voluntary movements. The most common causes of paralysis are stroke and spinal cord injuries. Paralysis can result in a partial or complete loss of control over movement, often leading to an unsteady gait. Side falls, a severe consequence of this imbalance, frequently cause broken bones and head injuries. Real-time gait monitoring with integrated analysis could greatly improve the rehabilitation process for such patients. The proposed smart insole is designed to provide real-time and remote gait monitoring for paralyzed individuals. This innovative approach holds promise for enhancing personalized rehabilitation programs and enabling early detection of impaired movement and balance control.This study will assess various locomotion scenarios to detect potential gait impairments and early signs of balance loss. A smart insole, featuring multiple sensors precisely designed and strategically placed, is developed to measure key gait parameters. A proof-of-concept model of the insole has been created to conduct experimental tests and demonstrate its functionality in different human activities. The model includes a 3D-printed insole equipped with a nano Arduino controller and integrated gyroscopes and accelerometers embedded in the insole. Additional sensors are positioned at specific locations to measure other critical parameters. A Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) sensor array is embedded in the insole to provide accurate, real-time detection of foot deformation, allowing for the identification of imbalances.

articleTitle: Primer on the Design and Construction of Quantum Circuits
abstract: Quantum algorithms promise up to a superpolynomial factor speedup in computational tasks compared to their classical counterparts. Quantum computers are now approaching sizes where quantum algorithms can be demonstrated. As a result, the implementation of algorithms as quantum circuits has become an important research topic. In this work, we provide an overview of quantum computation and the design of quantum circuits. Properties unique to quantum computation are outlined. We introduce how a quantum algorithm is translated into a circuit and show measures used to assess the performance of quantum circuits.

articleTitle: Two-Ended Fault Location in Transmission Lines with a Fault Current Limiting Reactor at One End
abstract: This paper presents an adaptation of two-ended impedance-based fault location algorithms for application in single-circuit transmission lines with a fault current limiting reactor (FCLR) installed at one terminal. The presence of an FCLR introduces additional impedance, complicating traditional fault location methods. The proposed methodology involves three steps: identifying the FCLR terminal and its impedance, calculating the effective voltage downstream of the FCLR, and applying conventional two-ended algorithms using the modified voltage and current phasors. The method is validated on a 138 kV transmission line.

articleTitle: Characterization of Photonically-Cured Semiconducting WS2 Films
abstract: Tungsten disulfide (WS<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) is a transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) that offers a wide range of potential applications given its electrical properties as a direct band gap semiconductor when in its mono-layer form. By using a photonic curing system (PCS), we can anneal thin-film substrates that contain two-dimensional (2D) materials within milliseconds without causing damage usually done by conventional thermal annealing treatments. In this experiment, we fabricate a device with chemically exfoliated WS<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> ink contacted with titanium (Ti) electrodes. The effect of photonic curing on the film’s electrical properties was analyzed for spin-coated WS<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> inks on a conventional thermally oxidized silicon (SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>/Si) substrate. We found that at given PCS conditions, we can increase the conductivity of the spin-cast film by over 200% through the current-voltage (I-V) measurements that were gathered. The Raman and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy measurements also reveal an enhancement in the peak positions of the respective peaks after photonically curing the films. Our initial results reveal that the properties of photonically-cured WS<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> can be enhanced, which will be useful in applying this emerging semiconducting material to future electronic and optoelectronic devices.

articleTitle: Real-Time Power Quality Classification Using a Raspberry Pi 3B+
abstract: Power quality monitoring is essential for maintaining the stability and efficiency of modern electrical systems worldwide. Traditional methods of monitoring power quality often require complex and expensive equipment, which is not always accessible or feasible in resource-limited areas. Although the development of efficient machine learning models is crucial, their true value lies in demonstrating their practical implementation on devices with limited resources. Building upon our previous work, this paper presents a novel approach for real-time power quality classification using the Large-EPQC model, deployed on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ edge device. By optimizing computational performance, the model accurately classifies power disturbances, offering a scalable and cost-efficient solution for real-world applications.

articleTitle: Robustness of triple-cation perovskite photo-absorbers under exposure to gamma-ray radiation
abstract: Halide perovskites have now garnered significant attention for their attractive photoabsorption features, including in detectors and solar cells. Their photoabsorption robustness in high, ambient radiation particularly ionizing gamma radiation (γ-ray), is also highly relevant for certain applications in nuclear-rich environments. In this work, we provide an initial assessment of triple-cation perovskites (TCPs) with the specific formulation comprised of Cs<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.05</inf>FA<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.79</inf>MA<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.16</inf>PbI<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2.45</inf>Br<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.55</inf>, after exposure to γ-ray radiation. The TCP’s characterization includes examining photoluminescence (PL) emission of spin-cast films, while the optoelectronic measurements of the photocurrent (I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ph</inf>) showed the devices to be relatively robust after exposure to the ambient radiation. This preliminary study is an initial step to continue to examine the intrinsic properties TCPs under exposure to ionizing radiation for next generation detectors, and related device applications.

articleTitle: Variable Temperature Hot Casting Study of 2D Perovskite Thin Films
abstract: Three-dimensional perovskites (3DP) have soared to the forefront of modern thin-film solar cell technology owing to their remarkable optoelectronic properties. These properties allow the creation of devices with power conversion efficiencies exceeding 27% steadily approaching the Shockley-Quesser limit. Despite these positive characteristics, 3DP are often inadequate and degrade when subjected to environmental conditions such as changes in temperature, moisture levels, or even sunlight itself. Ruddlesden-Popper phase two-dimensional perovskite (2DP) films are a direct counterpart to 3D perovskites and have shown great stability when compared to 3DP. However, 2DP-based devices tend to suffer from problems attributed to inherent poor charge transport characteristics caused by organic cations which act like spacers between the conductive inorganic layers. To improve charge transport we can improve the morphology of the 2DP, ideally making the film near single-crystalline quality. Near single crystal perovskites have a strongly preferential out-of-plane alignment with respect to contacts in planar devices facilitating improved charge transport. In this article, we report on how changes in temperature, specifically during fabrication, can affect the crystallography of 2DP. To examine film morphology after production, both optical and SEM images were taken of each fabricated device showing uniform films as well as unique amorphous structures. Photoluminescent spectroscopy (PL) was performed for each annealing temperature illustrating a red shift with increasing temperatures. I/V measurements were also taken to monitor the charge transport characteristics of each respective film with current levels in the nA range. An increase in current is noted from 100 to 145 degrees Celsius before dropping down at higher temperatures. Lastly, solar cells were fabricated with 2DP absorber layers hot casted at various temperatures with the peak PCE at around 2%.
